```{r ex-z-check}
"z = (x - mean) / sd, applied to the whole vector in one line."
```

## Toolbox B · Data frames and slicing

*Optional reference, using the neurite outgrowth data.*

### The neurite story

Neurites are the projections that grow out of a neuron's cell body. In the old
course scenario, neurite outgrowth was measured in cell cultures after two
differentiation treatments and in untreated controls, and exported to a CSV with
three columns: `control`, `condition_1`, `condition_2` (20 values each). The data
are synthetic; units are not documented. Rows are **not** matched: row 1 of
`control` and row 1 of `condition_1` are different cultures.

### Build a tiny data frame by hand

```{r df-demo, exercise=TRUE}
df_demo <- data.frame(
  control     = c(0.45, 0.62, 0.51),
  condition_1 = c(0.60, 0.70, 0.66),
  condition_2 = c(0.80, 0.77, 0.83)
)
df_demo
class(df_demo)
nrow(df_demo); ncol(df_demo); dim(df_demo)
str(df_demo)
```

```{r df-demo-solution}
df_demo <- data.frame(
  control     = c(0.45, 0.62, 0.51),
  condition_1 = c(0.60, 0.70, 0.66),
  condition_2 = c(0.80, 0.77, 0.83)
)
str(df_demo)
```

### Import and inspect the neurite file

```{r neurites-import, exercise=TRUE}
neurites <- read.csv("data/neurites.csv")
head(neurites)
dim(neurites)
colnames(neurites)
str(neurites)
summary(neurites)
```

```{r neurites-import-solution}
neurites <- read.csv("data/neurites.csv")
summary(neurites)
```

The `neurites` data frame is preloaded in every window below.

### Three ways to pick columns, one way to pick rows

`$` by name; `[ , "name"]` by name inside square brackets; `[ , 1]` by position.
The comma separates **rows** (before) from **columns** (after); leaving one side
empty means "all".

```{r slicing, exercise=TRUE}
neurites$control
neurites[ , "condition_1"]
neurites[ , 1:2]
neurites[ , c("control", "condition_2")]
neurites[1:5, ]                  # first five rows, all columns
neurites[1:2, c("control", "condition_2")]
```

```{r slicing-solution}
neurites[1:2, c("control", "condition_2")]
```

### Logical filters

A comparison gives a logical vector; using it as the row index keeps the rows
where it is `TRUE`. `&` means AND, `|` means OR.

```{r filters, exercise=TRUE}
neurites$control > 0.5
neurites[neurites$control > 0.5, ]
neurites[neurites$condition_1 > neurites$control & neurites$condition_2 > neurites$control, ]
```

```{r filters-solution}
neurites[neurites$control > 0.5, ]
```

**Exercise:** print the rows where `control` is greater than 0.2 **and**
`condition_1` is greater than 1.

```{r ex-filter, exercise=TRUE}

```

```{r ex-filter-hint}
# neurites[ CONDITION_A & CONDITION_B , ]
```

```{r ex-filter-solution}
neurites[neurites$control > 0.2 & neurites$condition_1 > 1, ]
```

```{r ex-filter-check}
"Combine the two comparisons with & inside the row position of [ , ]."
```

### Add a new column

```{r new-column, exercise=TRUE}
neurites$delta_1 <- neurites$condition_1 - neurites$control
head(neurites)
```

```{r new-column-solution}

head(neurites)
```

Use `neurites`. Each window checks the last line.

b. Compute mean, SD, median and quartiles of `condition_2` (the "same statistics for the other columns" exercise).



```{r ex-describe-check}
"End with the quantile() line."
```

c. **Challenge:** create a logical column `is_best2` that is `TRUE` when `condition_2` is greater than both `control` and `condition_1`. Then count with `table()`.

```{r ex-best2, exercise=TRUE}
neurites$is_best2 <- ___
table(neurites$is_best2)
```

```{r ex-best2-hint}
# neurites$condition_2 > neurites$control & neurites$condition_2 > neurites$condition_1
```

```{r ex-best2-solution}

  neurites$condition_2 > neurites$condition_1

```

```{r ex-best2-check}
"Two comparisons joined by &. table() on the last line."
```

```{r q-comma, results="asis"}
mcq("What does neurites[neurites$control > 0.5, ] return?",
    c("The control column only",
      "All columns, but only the rows where control exceeds 0.5",
      "An error, because nothing follows the comma"),
    2, "Rows before the comma, columns after. Empty after the comma means every column.")
```

<details><summary>🔍 Deeper: wide versus long tables</summary>

`neurites` is **wide**: one column per group. Many R functions (and `ggplot2`)
prefer **long** format: one row per observation with a `values` column and a
group column. Base R converts with `stack(neurites)`; the `reshape2` and `tidyr`
packages offer `melt()` and `pivot_longer()` for the same job. Notice that our MMSE table was already long. Long format is
the natural shape when every row is one observation.

```r
long_neurites <- stack(neurites)     # columns: values, ind
head(long_neurites)
```

</details>

### Saving a figure as a PDF

In an R Markdown document the figures are embedded automatically. For a standalone figure,
open a PDF "device", draw, and close it. A forgotten `dev.off()` leaves the
device open and later plots vanish into the file.

```{r gallery-pdf, exercise=TRUE}
pdf(file = "neurites_plot.pdf", width = 6, height = 4)
boxplot(neurites, col = c("lightblue", "lightgreen", "lightcoral"))
dev.off()
list.files(pattern = "pdf")     # the file now exists in the working directory
```

```{r gallery-pdf-solution}
boxplot(neurites, col = c("lightblue", "lightgreen", "lightcoral"))
dev.off()
```

### The same plots in ggplot2

`ggplot2` builds a plot from layers and wants **long** data. `aes()` maps columns
to axes and colours; `geom_*()` layers add bars, points, boxes; `+` stacks layers.

```{r gg-setup}
long_neurites <- stack(neurites)
names(long_neurites) <- c("value", "condition")
```

```{r gg-bar, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="gg-setup"}
library(ggplot2)
head(long_neurites)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = condition, y = value)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", fill = "lightblue", colour = "black")
```

```{r gg-bar-solution}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = condition, y = value, fill = condition)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", colour = "black") +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r gg-hist, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="gg-setup"}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 15)            # pooled
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = value, fill = condition)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ condition) + theme_classic()                                  # one panel per group
```

```{r gg-hist-solution}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = value, fill = condition)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, colour = "black") + facet_wrap(~ condition) + theme_classic()
```

```{r gg-box, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="gg-setup"}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = condition, y = value, fill = condition)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0) +
  labs(x = "Condition", y = "Neurite measurement (synthetic units)") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r gg-box-hint}
# Replace geom_boxplot() with geom_violin() and keep the jittered points.
# Delete the boxplot layer to get a pure jitter (strip) plot.
```

```{r gg-box-solution}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = condition, y = value, fill = condition)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0) +
  labs(x = "Condition", y = "Neurite measurement (synthetic units)") +
  theme_bw()
```

<details><summary>🔍 Deeper: ridge plots and ggsave</summary>

Another option is the **density ridge plot** from the `ggridges` package
(one smoothed density per group, stacked like a mountain range):

```r
install.packages("ggridges")
library(ggridges)
ggplot(long_neurites, aes(x = value, y = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_density_ridges() + theme_bw()
```

`ggsave("my_plot.pdf")` saves the most recent ggplot to a file.

</details>

```{r q-gallery, results="asis"}
mcq("A reviewer asks you to show the variability in each group and the sample size. Which figure is the weakest choice?",
    c("Boxplot with jittered points",
      "Bar chart of means without error bars or points",
      "Violin plot with points"),
    2, "Bars hide everything except one number per group.")
```

## Extras · More tests, for later

*Optional material. Not required today.*

### Student versus Welch, and the F-test

The classic Student t-test assumes equal variances in both groups
(`var.equal = TRUE`). An older recipe first runs an **F-test** (`var.test()`) to
compare the two variances and then chooses. Modern practice skips that gate: Welch
is safe either way, and the F-test itself is fragile with skewed data. Run all
three and compare the p-values and degrees of freedom.

```{r ftest, exercise=TRUE}
var.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1)
t.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1, var.equal = TRUE)    # Student
t.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1)                      # Welch (default)
```

```{r ftest-solution}
var.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1)
t.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1, var.equal = TRUE)
t.test(neurites$control, neurites$condition_1)
```

**Exercise:** run the t-test for `condition_2` versus `control` and store it as `test_2vsC`. Print its p-value alone with `$p.value`.

```{r ex-ttest2, exercise=TRUE}

```

```{r ex-ttest2-hint}
# test_2vsC <- t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$control)
# test_2vsC$p.value
```

```{r ex-ttest2-solution}
test_2vsC <- t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$control)
test_2vsC$p.value
```

```{r ex-ttest2-check}
"Put condition_2 first, control second, and finish with $p.value."
```

### Fold change and log2 fold change

Biologists often report a **ratio** of group means (fold change), especially
for expression data. A ratio only makes sense when zero means "nothing"
(a ratio scale). Neurite outgrowth qualifies; an MMSE score does not.

```{r fold-change, exercise=TRUE}
mean(neurites$condition_1) - mean(neurites$control)   # difference
mean(neurites$condition_1) / mean(neurites$control)   # fold change
log2(mean(neurites$condition_1) / mean(neurites$control))
```

```{r fold-change-hint}
# Repeat for condition_2. Which treatment has the larger effect? Which has more variability?
```

```{r fold-change-solution}
fc1 <- mean(neurites$condition_1) / mean(neurites$control)
fc2 <- mean(neurites$condition_2) / mean(neurites$control)
c(fold_change_1 = fc1, fold_change_2 = fc2)
log2(c(fc1, fc2))
sapply(neurites, sd)
```

```{r q-fold, results="asis"}
mcq("Condition 2 has a larger fold change than condition 1 but also a much larger SD. What does that tell you?",
    c("Condition 2 is simply better",
      "The average effect is larger, but individual cultures respond very differently; both the estimate and its uncertainty matter",
      "The data for condition 2 must be wrong"),
    2, "Look at the CI of each comparison: a large variable effect can be less certain than a smaller consistent one.")
```

### More than two groups

A one-way **ANOVA** asks whether all group means are equal; it does not say
which groups differ. **Kruskal–Wallis** is its rank-based cousin. Follow-up
pairwise comparisons form a family and need multiplicity control.

```{r three-groups, exercise=TRUE}
long_neurites <- stack(neurites)
oneway.test(values ~ ind, data = long_neurites, var.equal = FALSE)   # Welch ANOVA
kruskal.test(values ~ ind, data = long_neurites)
```

```{r three-groups-solution}
long_neurites <- stack(neurites)
oneway.test(values ~ ind, data = long_neurites, var.equal = FALSE)
kruskal.test(values ~ ind, data = long_neurites)
```

```{r three-comparisons, exercise=TRUE}
raw_p <- c(
  c1_vs_control = t.test(neurites$condition_1, neurites$control)$p.value,
  c2_vs_control = t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$control)$p.value,
  c2_vs_c1      = t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$condition_1)$p.value
)
data.frame(raw_p, bonferroni = p.adjust(raw_p, method = "bonferroni"))
```

```{r three-comparisons-solution}
raw_p <- c(
  c1_vs_control = t.test(neurites$condition_1, neurites$control)$p.value,
  c2_vs_control = t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$control)$p.value,
  c2_vs_c1      = t.test(neurites$condition_2, neurites$condition_1)$p.value
)
data.frame(raw_p, bonferroni = p.adjust(raw_p, method = "bonferroni"))
```

### Categorical data: the chi-square test

When both variables are categories, we compare **counts**. This invented 2×2
table records whether an assay detected a marker in two independent groups.
Inspect the expected counts: if any is below 5, use Fisher's exact test.

```{r chisq, exercise=TRUE}
counts <- matrix(c(18, 12, 9, 21), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                 dimnames = list(group = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                                 marker = c("Detected", "Not detected")))
counts
chisq.test(counts)
chisq.test(counts)$expected
```

```{r chisq-hint}
# fisher.test(counts) gives an exact p-value for small tables.
# With real data you build the table with table(data$var1, data$var2).
```

```{r chisq-solution}
counts <- matrix(c(18, 12, 9, 21), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                 dimnames = list(group = c("Control", "Treatment"),
                                 marker = c("Detected", "Not detected")))
chisq.test(counts)
fisher.test(counts)
```

```{r q-chisq, results="asis"}
mcq("Which question calls for a chi-square test?",
    c("Is the mean MMSE different between groups?",
      "Is dementia status associated with sex in this sample?",
      "Is age correlated with brain volume?"),
    2, "Chi-square compares observed counts in categories with the counts expected if the two variables were independent.")
```

### Paired observations

The same eight units measured before and after treatment. Pairing comes from the
design, never from two vectors happening to have the same length. A paired
t-test analyses the within-unit **changes**.

```{r paired, exercise=TRUE}
before <- c(10, 12, 8, 14, 11, 9, 13, 10)
after  <- c(11, 14, 8, 17, 12, 11, 14, 12)
change <- after - before
change
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
```

```{r paired-solution}
before <- c(10, 12, 8, 14, 11, 9, 13, 10)
after  <- c(11, 14, 8, 17, 12, 11, 14, 12)
change <- after - before
qqnorm(change); qqline(change)
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
```

```{r q-paired, results="asis"}
mcq("Eight participants are measured before and after treatment. Which statement is right?",
    c("Treat the 16 measurements as 16 separate people",
      "Use the pairing: analyse the eight within-person changes",
      "Pairing can be assumed whenever two columns have equal length"),
    2, "Pairing removes between-person variability and answers 'did individuals change?'. The design and the IDs establish it.")
```

## Command card and references

### Command card

Everything you need for today's questions. `d`, `x`, `y` and `g` are placeholders
for your own objects. Entries marked **(new)** did not appear on the Day 1 card.

| Need | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Store values | `x <- c(27, 28, 30)` |
| Import | `d <- read.csv("data/alzheimer_data.csv", header = TRUE)` |
| First look | `head(d)`; `dim(d)`; `nrow(d)`; `ncol(d)`; `names(d)`; `str(d)`; `summary(d)` |
| What type is a column? | `class(d$Age)`; `str(d)` |
| Distinct values of a column | `unique(d$CDR)` **(new)** |
| One column / one group | `d$MMSE`; `d$MMSE[d$Group == "Demented"]` |
| Rows and columns | `d[rows, cols]`; `d[d$MMSE < 20, ]`; `d[d$Group == "Demented" & d$sex == "M", ]` |
| Counts | `table(d$Group)`; `table(d$sex, d$Group)` |
| Missing values | `sum(is.na(d$SES))`; `colSums(is.na(d))` **(new)**; `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; `x[!is.na(x)]` |
| Add a column | `d$is_senior <- d$Age > 80` |
| Summaries | `mean(x)`; `median(x)`; `sd(x)`; `min(x)`; `max(x)`; `range(x)` **(new)**; `quantile(x)`; `IQR(x)` |
| Round a number | `round(x, digits = 2)` **(new)** |
| Summaries per group | `tapply(d$Age, d$Group, mean)`; `tapply(d$Age, d$Group, sd)` |
| Every column at once | `sapply(d, class)`; `sapply(d, mean)` |
| The row with the highest / lowest value | `d[which.min(d$MMSE), ]`; `d[which.max(d$MMSE), ]` **(new)** |
| Distribution plots | `hist(x)`; `boxplot(y ~ g, data = d)`; `stripchart(y ~ g, data = d, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter", add = TRUE, pch = 16)` |
| Bar chart of group means | `barplot(tapply(d$MMSE, d$Group, mean))` **(new)** |
| Scatterplot | `plot(d$nWBV, d$MMSE, pch = 16)` |
| Colour points by group | `col = c("red", "blue")[factor(d$Group)]` **(new)** |
| Add a legend | `legend("topright", legend = levels(factor(d$Group)), col = c("red", "blue"), pch = 16)` **(new)** |
| Several plots in one window | `par(mfrow = c(2, 2))` **(new)** |
| Normality evidence | `qqnorm(x); qqline(x)`; `shapiro.test(x)` |
| Two groups, two vectors | `t.test(x, y)`; `wilcox.test(x, y, exact = FALSE)` |
| Two groups, one column + one grouping column | `t.test(MMSE ~ Group, data = d)`; `wilcox.test(MMSE ~ Group, data = d)` **(new)** |
| Paired | `t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)` |
| More than two groups | `oneway.test(y ~ g, data = d)`; `kruskal.test(y ~ g, data = d)` |
| Association | `cor.test(x, y, method = "pearson")`; `cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)` |
| Categories | `table(a, b)`; `chisq.test(counts)`; `chisq.test(counts)$expected`; `fisher.test(counts)` |
| Pull one number out of a test | `t.test(x, y)$p.value`; `$conf.int`; `$estimate` |
| Multiple testing | `p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni")` |
| ggplot version | `ggplot(d, aes(nWBV, MMSE, colour = Group)) + geom_point()` |

### The result sentence

"In this sample (n = … per group), the estimated … minus … difference in mean …
was … units (95% CI … to …, Welch's t-test, p = …). The plots show …. This
supports … under the assumption that …; it does not show …."
